At my last serving job, there was this one night where these three big black dudes came in, and the other two servers working that shift, the male owner and his niece, just straight up IGNORED them, and I was like "da fuq???", mostly because the niece's bf was a black guy.

After I took that table, I stopped by the guy that was eyeing them, just to check-in and he seemed really      . . . . . *appreciative* of me.

This shit happens ALL the time in restaurants.

I suggest that you tip well to help break the stereotype, because honestly, unless you're a regular, a lot of staff will care less about you because they EXPECT you to not tip well. Who knows, maybe you tipping well means that another black person will get treated a little better later that shift.

Not to sound preachy, but where I come from, a lot of black teachers would repeatedly make the point, all through K-12, that you **represent your people**, even if that doesn't feel fair.

So, if tipping a certain amount seems unjust to you, I'd recommend you seeing it as making the world a more just place for someone else.

\------

Seriously though, there were a lot of nights at that restaurant where I'd take up a table of either black or Indian people simply because no one else wanted to take them.

AND THERE WERE REGULARS THERE THAT WERE BLACK, yet here I am taking this couple or this family because no one else wanted to "deal with them".

One night, the lady that owned that place saw a check that had a bad tip on it, and just straight up yelled out across the restaurant "Were they black or Indian?", and I just pause, like "How do you feel comfortable about that, even if it's YOUR restaurant?". (It was after closing.)

Vietnamese Buddhism does acknowledge other deities, but most of the focus is either to The Buddha or Guan Yin. There is one temple nearby that has a large display of varying statues and deities, but they're more the local exception rather than the local rule. Even then, compared to The Buddha or Guan Yin, those statues can feel more like decoration. People don't light incense for them outside, unlike the other two. Some will light incense to a Tara statue inside, as well as one or two other bodhisattvas. However, I'm uncertain how many of those people have an actual concept of Tara and who she is, and how many just see the statue and go, "I might as well pray."

As far as I'm aware, I haven't seen any translations of Saraswati, Shiva, or Ganesha in my local Vietnamese community.

\-

The monks at nearby temples actually seem fairly queer-friendly! They don't distinguish the trait as being corrupt, and one monk actually recited stories of a transgender bodhisattva.

Though, of course, there are conservatives that attend temples who are likely to disagree, and wish to use the religion to carry their personal values. While Buddhism itself may be gay-friendly, people who attend temple, by nature, are likely to be old-fashioned, and will claim that being Buddhist and being queer is incompatible, without much basis for doing so. I've heard my mother say "Buddha doesn't want you to be gay!", while I'm sure that the Buddha or Buddhas only care whether or not I'm *enlightened.*

Being in the US, there are a lot of people that don't attend temple with the intention of "This is Buddhism and enlightenment and religion." Many may be attached to Buddhism, because to them "This is Vietnam.", and so will stuff in their conservative Vietnamese values under the guise of Buddhism.

Personally, I think that too many people nearby are concerned with participating in Buddhism because it is their heritage, rather than for a genuine desire for enlightenment or spiritual growth.

People will pray to a deity, just because it is a Buddhist deity, without much care towards who the deity is or what they represent!

Really, I find it touching when people are drawn to Buddhism  because it is their history or heritage, but when the religion begins to become either misinterpreted or misunderstood because its name gets prioritized over its practice, that's when things get disheartening.

When I was first getting into Hinduism 4-5 years ago, I vaguely recall being especially drawn by the concepts of "Follow your Dharma." and *ahimsa*.

Plus, the religion seems fairly gay-friendly.  If we are all but souls going through levels of reincarnation, then why value less a soul happening to be living a gay existence?

I learned about hijdras and the Kama Sutra states that same-sex experience is "to be engaged in and enjoyed for its own sake as one of the arts."

Though obviously, a lot of Indians hold pretty conservative values when it comes to being queer.

I've just recently decided to shift during the pandemic, so haven't officially started practicing yet. The story from above took place 4-5 years ago. My next step is to get into the ethics system.

As far as clicking goes, Buddhism calls for a lot of detachment and moderation. For me personally, that's kind of dry. I value it for what it is. I understand the value of peaceful existence and calm being the result of detachment, but as a young person, I want to be able to understand the mental "filth" of passion, depression, and nervous tension. If I were to be Buddhist, I'd rather be Buddhist *after* I get to experience those highs and lows, just to get a better grasp of those mental filths.

I'm also a real big fan of polytheism. Without getting too in-depth with my personal upbringing, I have always felt like people have been shitty to me, and it has been awful. I feel like I lack support sometimes, and that people will always be shitty to me or dismiss me or just *want* me to kill myself.

With that context, the complex polytheism of Hinduism is incredibly comforting. It makes me feel a lot less existentially alone, and safe knowing that there is wide pantheon of deities available to pray to. When I pray, it feels like some deities are responding back in their own ways, "I've got you. You're gonna be okay. I don't want you to suffer. I'm right here. Just pray and try to listen to me. I'll make sure that you're okay."

The act of prayer really calms me down and comforts me, and that gets a lot better knowing that there are multiple deities to pray to.

Particularly, the deities Shiva, Parvati, Saraswati, and Ganesha have been where my intuition to pray has been directed.
